subject: Space
heading: You are seeing the sun as it was eight minutes ago
body: Light takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross 150 million km. If it went out you would carry on reading in bright daylight for the length of a song.

subject: Space
heading: There is a planet where it rains glass, sideways
body: HD 189733b is cobalt blue and its winds run at 5,400 mph. The blue is silicate particles — glass — blown horizontally through the atmosphere.

subject: Space
heading: Saturn would float
body: It is less dense than water. Find an ocean big enough and the whole planet would sit on top of it.

subject: Space
heading: A day on Venus is longer than its year
body: It turns once every 243 Earth days and orbits in 225. The sun rises in the west, twice a year, very slowly.

subject: Animals
heading: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
body: Two pump to the gills, one to the body — and that one stops when they swim, which is why they prefer crawling.

subject: Animals
heading: A shrimp can boil water by clicking
body: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw fast enough to form a collapsing bubble that reaches thousands of degrees for a fraction of a millisecond.

subject: Animals
heading: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings
body: The last stretch of intestine has patches of differing elasticity that mould them. Cubes do not roll away, which matters if you mark territory with them.

subject: Animals
heading: One jellyfish can reverse its own ageing
body: Turritopsis dohrnii reverts to its juvenile stage under stress and starts again. In principle it need never die of old age.

subject: Animals
heading: Crows hold grudges, and tell their friends
body: They recognise individual human faces, remember who treated them badly, and pass the grievance to birds that were never there.

subject: Everyday
heading: Honey never goes off
body: Jars from Egyptian tombs are still edible. Too acidic and too dry for bacteria, and bees add an enzyme that makes hydrogen peroxide.

subject: Everyday
heading: Bananas are clones
body: Almost every banana sold is a Cavendish, grown from cuttings — genetically one plant. That is why a single fungus can threaten the entire crop, and did once before.

subject: Everyday
heading: Carrots were purple first
body: Orange ones were bred in the Netherlands in the 16th century. The colour you think of as natural is a few hundred years old.

subject: Everyday
heading: The QWERTY layout is not slowing you down
body: The jamming story outlived the typewriter. Tests against faster layouts find differences small enough to vanish with practice.

subject: Everyday
heading: Bubble wrap was invented as wallpaper
body: It failed. Then it was sold as greenhouse insulation. It failed again. Only on the third attempt did anyone think of packaging.

subject: History
heading: Zero was banned in Florence
body: India had a symbol for it by the 7th century; Europe resisted 400 years, and Florence outlawed it in 1299. A digit meaning nothing looked like a way to forge a ledger.

subject: History
heading: Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford began around 1096. Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325. Two things that feel like different eras overlapped by centuries.

subject: History
heading: Cleopatra lived closer to the moon landing than to the pyramids
body: The Great Pyramid was already 2,500 years old when she was born. She is 2,000 years from us.

subject: History
heading: The last execution by guillotine was in 1977
body: The same year Star Wars opened and the Apple II went on sale. France kept it until 1981.

subject: Language
heading: Every word for "brother" sounds the same
body: Bhrātṛ in Sanskrit, frater in Latin, bróðir in Norse. They did not borrow it — they inherited it from one language nobody wrote down, spoken 6,000 years ago.

subject: Language
heading: Quarantine is a length of time
body: Quaranta giorni — forty days. Venice held arriving ships that long during the plague, and the word carries the number inside it.

subject: Language
heading: "Nice" used to mean stupid
body: From Latin nescius, not-knowing. It drifted through foolish, fussy, precise, and only landed on pleasant in the 1700s.

subject: Body
heading: You replace your skeleton about every ten years
body: Osteoclasts dissolve old bone; osteoblasts lay down new. The shape stays, the material does not. You are the same skeleton the way a river is the same river.

subject: Body
heading: Your gut has more bacteria than you have cells
body: Roughly 38 trillion of them to 30 trillion of you. By headcount you are a minority in your own body.

subject: Body
heading: Nothing you touch is actually touching you
body: The floor holds you up by electromagnetic repulsion between electrons. What you feel as contact is a force at a distance.

subject: Earth
heading: Africa is bigger than every map has shown you
body: The USA, China, India and most of Europe fit inside it at once. Mercator stretches the poles to keep angles true and squashes the equator to pay for it.

subject: Earth
heading: The sky is blue for the reason sunsets are red
body: Air scatters short wavelengths hardest. At sunset the light crosses far more air, the blue is scattered away entirely, and what is left is what reaches you.

subject: Earth
heading: Ice floats, and almost nothing else does
body: Water expands when it freezes because the hydrogen bonds lock into a lattice with gaps. If it did not, lakes would freeze from the bottom and stay frozen.

subject: Earth
heading: Russia spans eleven time zones
body: When it is Monday morning in Kaliningrad it is Monday evening in Kamchatka. One country, one working day, twelve hours apart.

subject: Making
heading: Blue was the most expensive colour for 600 years
body: Ultramarine came from lapis lazuli, mined in one valley in Afghanistan. It cost more than gold, which is why painters saved it for the Virgin Mary robes.

subject: Making
heading: An octave is a doubling
body: The A above middle C is 440 vibrations a second; the next A is 880. Every octave doubles, and that ratio is why they sound like the same note.

subject: Making
heading: The Eiffel Tower is taller in summer
body: Iron expands. It grows about 15cm on a hot day and leans slightly away from the sun.

subject: Study
heading: Reading it twice is one of the weakest ways to learn
body: Recall beats review: shut the book, write what you remember, then check. It feels worse and works better, which is exactly why people avoid it.

subject: Study
heading: Sleep is when the learning gets filed
body: The hippocampus replays the day during deep sleep and hands it to the cortex. Revising until 2am and sitting the paper at 9 skips the step that makes it stick.

subject: Study
heading: Spacing beats cramming at equal total time
body: Six hours over six days beats six hours in one. Each time you nearly forget and then retrieve it, the memory is rebuilt stronger.

subject: Money
heading: The £ sign is a letter L
body: Libra — Roman for pound weight. The two strokes through it mean abbreviation. Same root as lb for pounds, which is why neither looks like the word it stands for.

subject: Money
heading: A Post Office was once the biggest bank in the country
body: Before high street banking reached most towns, the Post Office Savings Bank held more accounts than every bank combined. It is why post offices still feel institutional.

subject: Money
heading: Nobody agrees what a billion is
body: It meant a million million in Britain until the 1970s and a thousand million in America. The government switched officially in 1974 and old textbooks did not.

subject: Sport
heading: The marathon distance comes from a royal box
body: It was 25 miles until London 1908, when the start moved to Windsor Castle so the children could watch from the nursery. The extra 385 yards has been standard ever since.

subject: Sport
heading: Football nearly had no crossbar
body: Until 1875 the goal was two posts and a tape. Teams argued endlessly about whether a ball had passed over or under it, which is a fair description of most sport before rules.

subject: Sport
heading: Table tennis was banned in the Soviet Union for 20 years
body: Officials decided it was harmful to the eyes. The ban lasted from 1930 to 1950, by which time the rest of the world had a considerable head start.

subject: Tech
heading: The first computer bug was a moth
body: Grace Hopper taped it into the Harvard Mark II logbook in 1947 with the note "first actual case of bug being found". The word already meant a fault; she found a literal one.

subject: Tech
heading: Wi-Fi does not stand for anything
body: A branding agency invented it to sound like hi-fi. IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence is what it replaced, and the meaninglessness was the point.

subject: Tech
heading: The @ sign was nearly extinct
body: It survived on typewriter keyboards as an accounting shorthand — 3 widgets @ £2. Ray Tomlinson picked it for email in 1971 because nobody used it in names.

subject: Tech
heading: Nokia started as a paper mill
body: Then rubber boots, then cables, then phones. Companies that last a century rarely do it by staying in the same business.

subject: Nature
heading: Trees talk through fungus
body: Mycorrhizal networks link roots across a forest, moving sugar and warning signals between trees. A dying tree will push its carbon into its neighbours.

subject: Nature
heading: A single aspen colony can be one organism
body: Pando in Utah is 47,000 trunks sharing one root system, thought to weigh 6,000 tonnes. It is possibly the heaviest living thing on Earth.

subject: Nature
heading: Bamboo can grow nearly a metre a day
body: Some species add 90cm in 24 hours — fast enough that you could watch it if you were patient. It is a grass, not a tree.

subject: Nature
heading: Lightning is five times hotter than the sun
body: About 30,000°C at the channel, against 5,500°C at the sun surface. Only for a few millionths of a second, which is the only reason anyone survives being near it.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Empire State Building went up in 410 days
body: Finished ahead of schedule and under budget in 1931. Modern equivalents take four or five years, and mostly for reasons that have nothing to do with the building.

subject: Buildings
heading: Notre-Dame took nearly 200 years
body: Begun 1163, largely finished 1345. Nobody who laid the first stone saw the roof. Cathedrals were built by people who accepted they would not see the end.

subject: Buildings
heading: Venice is built on wooden piles that never rotted
body: Millions of alder trunks driven into the mud. Without oxygen the wood petrified instead of decaying, and it has held the city up for 1,200 years.

subject: People
heading: The inventor of the Pringles tube is buried in one
body: Fredric Baur was so pleased with it that he asked to be interred in one. His children stopped at a supermarket on the way to the funeral to buy the tube.

subject: People
heading: Nikola Tesla died owing money in a New York hotel
body: He had 300 patents and had lit the world, and spent his last years feeding pigeons. Being right and being paid are different achievements.

subject: People
heading: Roald Dahl helped invent a brain valve
body: After his son was injured, he worked with an engineer and a surgeon on the Wade-Dahl-Till valve for hydrocephalus. It was used on thousands of children.

subject: Oddities
heading: There is a town where it is illegal to die
body: Longyearbyen in Svalbard. The permafrost stops bodies decomposing, so burials preserve whatever killed you — including the 1918 flu, still viable in graves there.

subject: Oddities
heading: A cloud weighs about 500 tonnes
body: An average cumulus holds roughly that much water. It stays up because the droplets are tiny and the air beneath is warmer and rising.

subject: Oddities
heading: The shortest war lasted 38 minutes
body: Britain against Zanzibar, 1896. The Sultan surrendered before the ships had finished firing, and the war was over before most people knew it had begun.

subject: Oddities
heading: Scotland has 421 words for snow
body: Feefle, flindrikin, snitter, spitters, unbrak. A language grows vocabulary where its speakers need precision, which is why English has so many words for rain.

subject: Space
heading: Saturn would float in a big enough bath
body: Its average density is about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre and water is 1.00. It is a ball of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface to stand on.

subject: Space
heading: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way
body: About three trillion trees against an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars. Both numbers are estimates, and they are not close enough for the comparison to be in doubt.

subject: Space
heading: Footprints on the Moon will outlast every building on Earth
body: There is no wind and no rain to move the dust. Only the slow rain of micrometeorites erodes them, over millions of years.

subject: Space
heading: Jupiter has a storm that has been running for centuries
body: The Great Red Spot has been watched since at least 1831 and probably since the 1660s. It is shrinking: it was twice as wide a hundred years ago.

subject: Space
heading: The International Space Station sees sixteen sunrises a day
body: It orbits at about 28,000 km/h and goes round the Earth every 90 minutes. Crews keep to Greenwich Mean Time so that meals and sleep still make sense.

subject: Space
heading: Space is silent because there is nothing to shake
body: Sound is a pressure wave in a material. With almost no particles between them, two astronauts a metre apart could shout and hear nothing.

subject: Space
heading: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh about a billion tonnes
body: A star heavier than the Sun is crushed into a ball the width of a city, so its atoms collapse into neutrons packed like an atomic nucleus.

subject: Space
heading: Olympus Mons is nearly three times the height of Everest
body: The Martian volcano stands about 22 km above the surrounding plains. Mars has no moving tectonic plates, so a volcano sits over its hot spot and keeps growing.

subject: Space
heading: The Moon is drifting away at about the speed a fingernail grows
body: 3.8 cm a year, measured by bouncing lasers off mirrors the Apollo crews left behind. Tides are slowing the Earth and the Moon takes the energy.

subject: Space
heading: Most of the Solar System is Sun
body: The Sun holds about 99.86% of all the mass in it. Jupiter is most of what is left, and everything else — planets, moons, asteroids — shares the remainder.

subject: Space
heading: Light from the nearest star takes over four years to get here
body: Proxima Centauri is 4.24 light years away. A car at motorway speed would need about fifty million years to make the trip.

subject: Space
heading: Astronauts get taller in orbit
body: Without gravity compressing the spine the discs between the vertebrae expand, adding up to 5 cm. It goes back within days of landing, often with backache.

subject: Space
heading: Mercury has ice, thirty million miles from the Sun
body: Craters at its poles never see sunlight, so their floors stay below −170 degrees Celsius and hold water ice while the day side reaches 430.

subject: Space
heading: Every atom heavier than iron was made in a dying star
body: Fusion in a star stops paying at iron. The gold in a ring and the iodine in your thyroid were forged in a supernova or a collision of neutron stars.

subject: Space
heading: Voyager 1 is carrying a record nobody can play without instructions
body: A gold-plated copper disc with sounds and pictures from Earth, plus a diagram showing how to spin it. It is now over 24 billion km away and still answering.

subject: Space
heading: Halley’s Comet comes back about every 76 years
body: It was last here in 1986 and is due in 2061. Most people get one chance at it, which is why every return is written down somewhere.

subject: Space
heading: The Sun makes a Hiroshima bomb of energy every millionth of a second
body: Fusion in the core turns about four million tonnes of mass into energy every second. It has been doing it for 4.6 billion years and is roughly halfway through.

subject: Animals
heading: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood
body: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one through the body. The blue comes from haemocyanin, which carries oxygen with copper where our blood uses iron.

subject: Animals
heading: A shrimp can punch hard enough to boil water
body: The mantis shrimp’s club accelerates like a bullet. The water behind it briefly vaporises into a bubble that collapses with a flash of light and a bang.

subject: Animals
heading: A tardigrade has survived being fired into open space
body: Dried out, it pulls in its legs and stops almost all chemistry. Samples flown on a 2007 mission came back alive after ten days of vacuum and raw sunlight.

subject: Animals
heading: Elephants cannot jump
body: Every other land mammal can get all four feet off the ground. An elephant’s legs are built as columns for carrying weight, with no springy tendon to push off with.

subject: Animals
heading: A honeybee visits about two million flowers for one jar of honey
body: A worker makes a twelfth of a teaspoon in her whole life. The hive flies the equivalent of twice round the world for a 450 gram jar.

subject: Animals
heading: Crows can recognise individual human faces and hold a grudge
body: Researchers in Seattle wore masks to trap crows, and birds scolded that mask for years. Birds that were never trapped learned to scold it too.

subject: Animals
heading: A sloth can take a month to digest one leaf
body: Its stomach has four chambers and its body runs cool to save energy. Two thirds of a well-fed sloth’s weight can be the contents of its gut.

subject: Animals
heading: The Greenland shark can live for four hundred years
body: Radiocarbon dating of the lens of the eye gave one female an estimated age near 392. They do not breed until about 150 years old.

subject: Animals
heading: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance
body: The pink is not theirs. They eat algae and brine shrimp full of carotenoids, and a flamingo fed a plain diet fades to white.

subject: Animals
heading: Cats cannot taste sweetness
body: The gene for one half of the sweet receptor is broken in every cat studied, from the house cat to the tiger. A pure carnivore has no use for it.

subject: Animals
heading: A hummingbird’s heart beats over 1,200 times a minute in flight
body: It has to eat roughly its own body weight in nectar every day, and at night it can drop into torpor with its heart at fifty beats a minute to survive.

subject: Animals
heading: Axolotls regrow legs, jaws and parts of the brain
body: They also stay larval for life, keeping feathery gills instead of turning into land salamanders. In the wild they survive in one lake system in Mexico City.

subject: Animals
heading: The blue whale’s call is louder than a jet engine
body: Up to 188 decibels, and low enough that it carries for hundreds of kilometres through deep water. The animal is the largest that has ever lived.

subject: Animals
heading: A snail can have thousands of teeth
body: They sit on a ribbon called a radula which it scrapes across surfaces like a file. A limpet’s teeth are the strongest natural material yet measured.

subject: Animals
heading: Reindeer eyes change colour with the season
body: A layer behind the retina is gold in the Arctic summer and deep blue in winter, scattering light back through the retina so the eye catches more of it.

subject: Animals
heading: Emperor penguin fathers go four months without eating
body: He balances the egg on his feet through the Antarctic winter, huddling in a crowd that slowly rotates so nobody is on the windward edge for long.

subject: Animals
heading: A pistol shrimp snaps its claw and stuns fish with the bubble
body: The claw shuts in under a millisecond. The jet of water it fires creates a cavitation bubble that collapses at thousands of degrees for a fraction of a second.

subject: Animals
heading: Ants do not have lungs
body: They breathe through holes along the body called spiracles, connected to tubes that carry air straight to the tissues. It works beautifully and only at small sizes.

subject: Maths
heading: In a room of 23 people it is more likely than not that two share a birthday
body: There are 253 possible pairs, not 23, and each pair is a chance. At 70 people it is 99.9%. Our intuition compares everybody to ourselves instead.

subject: Maths
heading: A piece of paper folded 42 times would reach the Moon
body: Each fold doubles the thickness, and 0.1 mm doubled 42 times is about 440,000 km. You cannot actually do it: the record is twelve folds.

subject: Maths
heading: There are more ways to shuffle a deck than there are atoms on Earth
body: 52 factorial is about 8 followed by 67 zeros. A well-shuffled deck has almost certainly never existed in that order before.

subject: Maths
heading: Zero took a long time to be a number
body: Babylonians used a gap, Greeks argued about whether nothing could be something, and the symbol arrived from India via the Islamic world around the 9th century.

subject: Maths
heading: Pi has been calculated to over a hundred trillion digits and NASA uses fifteen
body: Fifteen decimal places are enough to work out the circumference of the Solar System to within the width of a finger.

subject: Maths
heading: A Mobius strip has one side and one edge
body: Give a paper strip a half twist and glue the ends. Draw a line down the middle and you return to the start having covered what looked like both faces.

subject: Maths
heading: Doubling a rice grain per chessboard square needs more rice than exists
body: The 64th square alone is 9.2 million trillion grains. The whole board comes to about a thousand times the world’s annual rice crop.

subject: Maths
heading: The Fibonacci numbers show up in pine cones and sunflowers
body: Each number is the sum of the two before it. Seeds packed at the angle those numbers give leave the fewest gaps, so plants that do it fit more in.

subject: Maths
heading: Seventy per cent of numbers starting with 1 is normal, not suspicious
body: Benford’s law: in many real data sets the leading digit is 1 about 30% of the time and 9 about 5%. Tax offices use it to spot invented figures.

subject: Maths
heading: A four-colour map is always enough
body: No map of countries needs more than four colours for no two neighbours to match. Proved in 1976, and the first famous proof that needed a computer.

subject: Maths
heading: There is no biggest prime number
body: Euclid proved it around 300 BC in a few lines: multiply any finite list of primes together and add one, and you have a number none of them divides.

subject: Maths
heading: A circle is the shape that holds the most for the least edge
body: For a fixed perimeter nothing encloses more area. It is why a soap bubble is round, and why a cold animal curls up.

subject: Maths
heading: Your chances improve if you switch doors
body: The Monty Hall problem: pick one of three doors, the host opens a losing one, and switching wins two times in three. Almost everyone refuses to believe it.

subject: Maths
heading: Roman numerals have no zero and no place value
body: That is why long division in Rome was a specialist job. The Hindu-Arabic system we use puts the value in the position, so a clerk can do it with a pen.

subject: Maths
heading: The word algebra comes from an Arabic book title
body: Al-Khwarizmi’s 9th-century Kitab al-jabr. Al-jabr means restoring — moving a subtracted term to the other side. His name gave us the word algorithm.

subject: Maths
heading: A googol is bigger than the number of atoms in the observable universe
body: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros; the atom count is nearer 1 followed by 80. A nine-year-old named it, and a search engine misspelled it.

subject: Maths
heading: Two people in London almost certainly have exactly the same number of hairs
body: A head carries up to about 150,000 hairs and the city holds nine million people. More people than possible hair counts means at least two must match.

subject: Maths
heading: The equals sign was invented to save writing
body: Robert Recorde put two parallel lines in a book in 1557, because, he wrote, no two things can be more equal. Before that people wrote it out in words.

subject: Body
heading: Your stomach lining is replaced every few days
body: It has to be: the acid in there is strong enough to dissolve metal. The cells that make the protective mucus are among the fastest-renewing in the body.

subject: Body
heading: Bone is stronger than concrete for its weight
body: A cubic inch of bone can take about 8,600 kg in compression. It is also alive, rebuilding itself along the lines where it is loaded most.

subject: Body
heading: You have about 100,000 km of blood vessels
body: Mostly capillaries thin enough that red cells pass in single file. Laid end to end they would go round the Earth twice.

subject: Body
heading: The eye has a blind spot and the brain paints over it
body: Where the optic nerve leaves the retina there are no light receptors at all. What you see there is the brain’s best guess from the surroundings.

subject: Body
heading: Goosebumps are a leftover from having fur
body: Tiny muscles pull each hair upright to trap air and make an animal look bigger. On a nearly hairless body it achieves almost nothing.

subject: Body
heading: Half the cells you carry are not yours
body: Roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones, mostly in the large intestine. They weigh about the same as the brain and help digest what we cannot.

subject: Body
heading: A baby is born with about 300 bones and ends up with 206
body: Many start as separate pieces of cartilage and fuse as they grow. The skull plates stay separate at birth so the head can squeeze through.

subject: Body
heading: Your nose remaps smells while you sleep
body: Smell is the only sense that does not route through the thalamus on its way to consciousness, which is part of why a smell can return a memory so quickly.

subject: Body
heading: Fingerprints are not unique to humans
body: Koalas have prints so similar to ours that they have confused forensic examiners. Both species climb and grip, and the ridges probably help with touch.

subject: Body
heading: You cannot tickle yourself
body: The cerebellum predicts the sensation from your own movement and cancels it out. That prediction is how you can hold a cup without watching your hand.

subject: Body
heading: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day
body: Around 2.5 billion times in an average life, moving roughly 7,500 litres of blood every 24 hours without ever taking a rest day.

subject: Body
heading: The strongest muscle for its size is in your jaw
body: The masseter can close the back teeth with a force over 90 kg. The strongest by total force is the gluteus maximus, which is why you can climb stairs.

subject: Body
heading: Bruises change colour as your body takes the blood apart
body: Haemoglobin breaks down into biliverdin, which is green, then bilirubin, which is yellow. The colour tells you roughly how old the bruise is.

subject: Body
heading: You make about a litre and a half of saliva a day
body: It starts digestion before food reaches the stomach: the enzyme amylase in it begins breaking starch into sugar while you are still chewing.

subject: Body
heading: Your sense of balance lives in three loops of fluid in each ear
body: The semicircular canals sit at right angles to each other, so they can tell nodding from shaking from tilting. Spinning leaves the fluid moving after you stop.

subject: Body
heading: The cornea has no blood supply
body: It takes oxygen straight from the air, which is why a cornea can be transplanted with very little risk of rejection — there is no blood to carry the attack.

subject: Body
heading: Adults have about 5 litres of blood and give away under a tenth of it
body: A blood donation is 470 ml. The plasma is back within a day and the red cells within a few weeks, which is why you can give every three or four months.

subject: History
heading: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford is recorded from 1096. Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.

subject: History
heading: The shortest war in history lasted under an hour
body: Britain against Zanzibar, 27 August 1896. Estimates run from 38 to 45 minutes, and the Sultan’s palace was in ruins before lunch.

subject: History
heading: The Great Fire of London killed officially six people
body: It destroyed 13,200 houses and 87 churches. The low death toll is partly record-keeping: the poor were not always counted.

subject: History
heading: Napoleon was not short
body: He was about 5 feet 7 in modern measure, average for a Frenchman of his day. The confusion is French inches, which were longer than English ones.

subject: History
heading: Vikings did not wear horned helmets
body: No horned helmet has ever been found in a Viking grave. The image comes from a costume designer for a Wagner opera in 1876.

subject: History
heading: The first computer programmer wrote her programs before the computer existed
body: Ada Lovelace published an algorithm for Babbage’s Analytical Engine in 1843. The machine was never finished in her lifetime.

subject: History
heading: Ketchup was sold as medicine in the 1830s
body: An Ohio doctor claimed tomato pills cured indigestion and jaundice. The trade collapsed when competitors sold pills with no tomato in them at all.

subject: History
heading: The Tower of Pisa was leaning before it was finished
body: Building stopped for nearly a century after the third floor because of war. The pause let the ground settle, which is probably why it is still standing.

subject: History
heading: Wartime Britain invented a cover story about carrots
body: The story that carrots gave RAF pilots night vision helped hide the existence of airborne radar. Carrots do contain vitamin A, which the eye genuinely needs.

subject: History
heading: The Rosetta Stone is a tax decree
body: It repeats the same priestly decree in Greek, demotic and hieroglyphs. Comparing them is what let Champollion read hieroglyphs again after 1,400 years.

subject: History
heading: The Statue of Liberty arrived in 350 pieces
body: It came from France in 214 crates in 1885 and took four months to assemble. The copper skin is about the thickness of two pennies.

subject: History
heading: Postboxes in Britain were once green
body: They were painted green until 1874, then repainted red over about a decade because people kept walking into them.

subject: History
heading: Harvard was founded before calculus was invented
body: Harvard dates from 1636; Newton and Leibniz developed calculus in the 1660s and 1670s. The first students learned Latin, Greek and theology.

subject: History
heading: The Black Death moved about as fast as a person could walk
body: It crossed Europe in roughly four years from 1347. Fleas travelled on rats, and rats travelled on carts and ships at human pace.

subject: History
heading: The word salary comes from salt
body: Roman soldiers received an allowance connected with salt, called salarium. Salt was the only practical way to keep meat before refrigeration.

subject: History
heading: A Roman legionary carried about 30 kg on the march
body: Armour, shield, two javelins, a sword, a saw, a basket, a cooking pot and rations for days. They were nicknamed Marius’ mules for it.

subject: History
heading: The first email was sent in 1971 and nobody remembers what it said
body: Ray Tomlinson sent it between two computers side by side, and later said the text was probably QWERTYUIOP. He chose @ because it was not in anyone’s name.

subject: Earth
heading: The deepest hole ever drilled got a third of the way through the crust
body: The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12.26 km in 1989 and stopped because the rock was 180 degrees Celsius and behaving like plastic.

subject: Earth
heading: Mount Everest grows about 4 mm a year
body: India is still pushing into Asia at roughly 5 cm a year. Earthquakes can knock the summit down a little, and the 2015 Nepal quake did.

subject: Earth
heading: The Sahara was green within human history
body: Until about 5,000 years ago it held lakes, hippos and cattle herders. Rock paintings deep in the desert show people swimming.

subject: Earth
heading: There is a lake under Antarctica that has been sealed for millions of years
body: Lake Vostok lies under 4 km of ice, kept liquid by pressure and the heat of the rock below. It is about the size of Lake Ontario.

subject: Earth
heading: Iceland is getting wider
body: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs straight through it, so the two halves of the island are pulling apart by about 2 cm a year. You can walk down the gap at Thingvellir.

subject: Earth
heading: A day is getting longer, very slowly
body: Tidal friction adds about 1.7 milliseconds per century. In the Devonian, 400 million years ago, a year held about 400 days.

subject: Earth
heading: Most of the planet’s fresh water is frozen
body: About 69% is locked in ice caps and glaciers and nearly all of the rest is groundwater. Rivers and lakes hold well under 1% of it.

subject: Earth
heading: Volcanic lightning is real and nobody is entirely sure why
body: Ash particles rubbing together build up charge in the plume. Eruptions at Eyjafjallajokull and Taal produced storms of it over the crater.

subject: Earth
heading: The Dead Sea is so salty you cannot sink in it
body: About 34% salt against the ocean’s 3.5%. Nothing bigger than a microbe lives in it, and it is dropping over a metre a year as the Jordan is drawn off.

subject: Sea
heading: More of the Moon has been mapped than the deep ocean floor
body: About a quarter of the sea bed has been surveyed in detail by sonar. The rest is inferred from satellite measurements of the shape of the sea surface.

subject: Sea
heading: The Mariana Trench would swallow Everest with a mile to spare
body: Challenger Deep is about 10,935 m down. Only a handful of people have been to the bottom — fewer than have walked on the Moon.

subject: Sea
heading: Most of the oxygen you breathe came from the sea
body: Estimates put the plankton share at 50 to 80% of all the oxygen produced. One genus, Prochlorococcus, may make a fifth of it on its own.

subject: Sea
heading: Seawater is not the same blue everywhere and that is biology
body: Water absorbs red light first, which is why deep water looks blue. Green water is water full of chlorophyll, which is to say full of life.

subject: Sea
heading: There are rivers and lakes at the bottom of the sea
body: Brine pools are so much saltier than the water above that they sit in pools with a visible shoreline, and submersibles can watch waves lap at the edge.

subject: Sea
heading: The longest mountain range on Earth is underwater
body: The mid-ocean ridge runs about 65,000 km round the globe, where new sea floor is made as plates pull apart. Almost none of it has ever been seen.

subject: Sea
heading: A blue whale’s tongue can weigh as much as an elephant
body: Its heart is the size of a small car and its aorta is wide enough to crawl through. It feeds on krill a few centimetres long.

subject: Sea
heading: Sea otters hold hands so they do not drift apart
body: They wrap themselves in kelp for the same reason. They also keep a favourite stone in a pouch of loose skin under the arm for breaking shells.

subject: Science
heading: Glass is not a slow-moving liquid
body: Old window panes are thicker at the bottom because of how they were made, not because they flowed. At room temperature glass is a solid and stays one.

subject: Science
heading: Hot water can freeze faster than cold under the right conditions
body: The Mpemba effect has been reported since Aristotle and is still argued about. Evaporation, dissolved gas and convection all seem to play a part.

subject: Science
heading: A single bolt of lightning is five times hotter than the Sun’s surface
body: About 30,000 degrees Celsius against the Sun’s 5,500. The thunder is the air around it exploding outwards as it is heated in a fraction of a second.

subject: Science
heading: Helium was found on the Sun before it was found on Earth
body: A yellow line in the 1868 eclipse spectrum matched no known element, and it was named after Helios. It was isolated on Earth 27 years later.

subject: Science
heading: Diamonds and pencil lead are the same element
body: Both are pure carbon. In diamond each atom is bonded to four others in a rigid lattice; in graphite the atoms sit in sheets that slide over each other.

subject: Science
heading: Water expands when it freezes, which is why lakes freeze from the top
body: Almost every other substance contracts. Ice floating means the water below stays liquid, which is the only reason fish survive a winter.

subject: Science
heading: Atoms are almost entirely empty space
body: If the nucleus were a marble on a football pitch, the electrons would be at the stands. What stops your hand passing through a table is electrical repulsion.

subject: Science
heading: Absolute zero has never been reached
body: Minus 273.15 Celsius. Laboratories have got within a few billionths of a degree, but removing the last of the energy would take infinite steps.

subject: Science
heading: A superconductor will float above a magnet and stay there
body: Below a critical temperature it expels magnetic field entirely. Cooled in place, it locks to its position and can be pushed around a track without touching it.

subject: Science
heading: The tallest possible tree is about 130 metres and physics decides it
body: Above that, water cannot be pulled to the leaves against gravity and friction without the column breaking. The tallest measured redwood is 116 m.

subject: Science
heading: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air
body: 1,480 metres per second against 343. In steel it is faster again, which is why you can hear a train through a rail before you hear it through the air.

subject: Science
heading: Bananas are slightly radioactive
body: They are rich in potassium and one isotope of it, potassium-40, is unstable. The dose is tiny and your own body carries more of it than the fruit does.

subject: Science
heading: Rust is iron burning, very slowly
body: It is the same chemistry as a flame — oxidation — running at room temperature. Salt speeds it up because it carries the charge between the two reactions.

subject: Science
heading: Metals feel colder than wood at the same temperature
body: They conduct heat out of your hand faster. What you are feeling is not temperature at all but the rate at which your skin is losing heat.

subject: Science
heading: A gram of DNA could hold every film ever made
body: Researchers have stored and read back data in synthetic DNA at densities around 200 petabytes per gram. It also lasts thousands of years if kept dry and cold.

subject: Science
heading: The hottest chilli is measured by how much sugar water hides it
body: The Scoville scale began in 1912 as a taste test with a panel of people. Capsaicin binds the same receptor that responds to actual heat, which is why it burns.

subject: Science
heading: Nothing in the universe is truly at rest
body: You are turning with the Earth, orbiting the Sun at 30 km/s, going round the galaxy at 220, and moving with the galaxy through the local group.

subject: Language
heading: English has no word that rhymes with orange, month or silver
body: Purple has one — curple, an old word for a horse’s hindquarters. Rhyme is a fact about a language’s sound inventory rather than about the world.

subject: Language
heading: The dot over an i is called a tittle
body: It arrived in medieval manuscripts to stop i being lost among the strokes of m, n and u. The word survives mainly in the phrase jot or tittle.

subject: Language
heading: Shakespeare is the first recorded user of about 1,700 English words
body: Eyeball, bedazzled, lacklustre, swagger. Some he coined and some he simply wrote down first, which is a different claim and easier to prove.

subject: Language
heading: There is a language with no words for left and right
body: Guugu Yimithirr in Queensland uses compass directions for everything, including where a cup sits on a table. Its speakers keep a running sense of north.

subject: Language
heading: The longest word in most dictionaries is a lung disease
body: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis, 45 letters, coined in 1935 partly to be long. The disease itself is ordinarily called silicosis.

subject: Language
heading: Icelandic speakers can read texts written a thousand years ago
body: The language has changed so little that the medieval sagas are set books in school. New words are built from Icelandic roots rather than borrowed.

subject: Language
heading: The ampersand was once the 27th letter of the alphabet
body: Children finished by reciting "and per se and", which slurred into ampersand. The symbol itself is a cursive Latin et.

subject: Language
heading: Nearly half the world speaks a language descended from one prehistoric tongue
body: Proto-Indo-European was spoken perhaps 6,000 years ago and left no writing. It is reconstructed from the regular sound differences between its descendants.

subject: Language
heading: Sign languages are not signed versions of spoken ones
body: British and American Sign Language are unrelated and mutually unintelligible, with their own grammar. BSL is closer to Auslan than to ASL.

subject: Language
heading: Emoji began on a Japanese phone network in 1999
body: Shigetaka Kurita drew 176 symbols on a 12 by 12 grid for NTT DoCoMo. The originals are now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

subject: Language
heading: The word robot comes from a play about forced labour
body: Karel Capek’s R.U.R., Prague 1920, from the Czech robota. The robots in it are artificial people, and they win.

subject: Language
heading: Punctuation was invented to help people read aloud
body: Ancient Greek and Latin were written without spaces between words. Marks were added by scribes to show where a reader should breathe.

subject: Language
heading: Welsh has a word for the ache of longing for a place
body: Hiraeth: a homesickness for somewhere you may never have been, or that no longer exists. Portuguese saudade is close but not the same.

subject: Language
heading: Almost every language has a word like huh
body: A study of 31 unrelated languages found a short, low, questioning syllable in every one. It seems to be a repair tool for conversation rather than a word.

subject: Language
heading: The QWERTY layout was not designed to slow you down
body: That story is repeated everywhere. It was arranged to separate common letter pairs so the typebars of an 1870s machine would not jam into each other.

subject: Language
heading: A pangram uses every letter once and they are hard to write
body: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog has 35 letters for 26 slots. Perfect pangrams exist but read like a car registration.

subject: Everyday
heading: The plastic tip on a shoelace has a name
body: It is an aglet. Without one the fibres unravel and the lace will not thread, which is why they were made of metal before plastic.

subject: Everyday
heading: A pencil can draw a line about 56 km long
body: Roughly 45,000 words from one pencil, with no ink to dry out and nothing to leak at altitude. Graphite writes by leaving sheets of carbon on the paper.

subject: Everyday
heading: The microwave was invented by a man who noticed a melted chocolate bar
body: Percy Spencer was standing near a magnetron in 1945. He tried popcorn next, then an egg, which exploded over a colleague.

subject: Everyday
heading: Velcro was copied from burrs stuck to a dog
body: George de Mestral looked at them under a microscope in 1941 and found hooks. The name is from velours and crochet — velvet and hook.

subject: Everyday
heading: A cash machine PIN was four digits because of one man’s wife
body: John Shepherd-Barron proposed six and his wife said she could only remember four. Four has been the world standard ever since.

subject: Everyday
heading: The hole in a pen lid is there to stop you choking
body: It keeps an airway open if one is swallowed. BIC added it deliberately, and it is now required by safety standards for caps that size.

subject: Everyday
heading: Left-handed scissors are genuinely different, not marketing
body: The blades are swapped so the cutting edge you can see is the one that matters. With the wrong pair a left-hander pushes the blades apart and the paper folds.

subject: Everyday
heading: Toilet roll was sold with a warning that it was splinter-free
body: Early paper was made from wood pulp with the splinters still in it. Northern Tissue advertised splinter-free paper as a feature into the 1930s.

subject: Everyday
heading: A tin opener was invented 48 years after the tin
body: Cans were patented in 1810 and opened with a hammer and chisel. The instruction on early tins was to cut round the top with a chisel.

subject: Food
heading: Carrots were purple before they were orange
body: Orange carrots were selectively bred in the Netherlands in the 16th century. Purple, white and yellow varieties are still grown and taste much the same.

subject: Food
heading: A strawberry is not a berry and a banana is
body: Botanically a berry comes from a single ovary with seeds inside. A strawberry’s seeds are on the outside and each one is a separate fruit.

subject: Food
heading: Nutmeg was once worth more than its weight in gold
body: It grew on a handful of Indonesian islands and Europe fought wars over it. Britain traded one of them to the Dutch for Manhattan.

subject: Food
heading: Bread rises because yeast breathes out
body: Yeast eats sugar and gives off carbon dioxide and alcohol. The gluten network traps the gas in bubbles, and the alcohol bakes off in the oven.

subject: Food
heading: Peanuts are not nuts
body: They are legumes and grow underground, related to peas and beans. An almond is a seed inside a fruit, and a cashew grows outside one.

subject: Food
heading: Onions make you cry because they fight back
body: Cutting releases an enzyme that makes a sulphur compound which drifts up and reacts with the water in your eyes to form a small amount of sulphuric acid.

subject: Food
heading: Chocolate was a bitter drink for most of its history
body: The Maya and Aztec drank cacao spiced and unsweetened. Sugar and milk are European additions, and solid eating chocolate is only about 180 years old.

subject: Food
heading: Apples float because a fifth of an apple is air
body: That is why apple bobbing works at all. It is also why a bruised apple sinks a little lower: the damaged cells fill with juice.

subject: Food
heading: The hottest part of a chilli is not the seeds
body: It is the pale pith the seeds are attached to, where the capsaicin is made. Scraping out the pith takes most of the heat with it.

subject: Tech
heading: The Apollo computer had less memory than a musical birthday card
body: About 72 kilobytes of read-only memory and 4 kilobytes of working memory. It flew twelve people to the Moon and it was hand-woven from wire and magnets.

subject: Tech
heading: The first webcam watched a coffee pot
body: Cambridge computer scientists pointed a camera at the shared pot in 1991 so nobody climbed the stairs for nothing. It went online to the world in 1993.

subject: Tech
heading: A single Google search uses about as much energy as a lightbulb for a minute
body: The search itself is fast; the cost is in keeping thousands of machines warm and ready so the answer arrives in a fifth of a second.

subject: Tech
heading: The at sign is older than email by centuries
body: Merchants used it for "at the rate of" — 10 barrels @ £5. It survived on the typewriter keyboard, which is why it was free for Ray Tomlinson to borrow.

subject: Tech
heading: Wi-Fi came out of a failed attempt to detect exploding black holes
body: Australian radio astronomers built maths for untangling smeared signals. It did not find the black holes and it is now in the chip in every phone.

subject: Tech
heading: The first 1GB hard drive weighed 250 kg
body: IBM shipped it in 1980 and it cost around $40,000. The same capacity now fits on a chip smaller than a fingernail and costs less than a sandwich.

subject: Tech
heading: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king
body: Harald Bluetooth united Denmark and Norway; the logo is his initials in runes. It was a code name that nobody got round to replacing.

subject: Tech
heading: A QR code can lose 30% of itself and still work
body: It carries Reed-Solomon error correction, the same family of maths that keeps a scratched CD playing. The three big squares tell the scanner which way up it is.

subject: Tech
heading: Undo was invented in the 1970s and changed how people use computers
body: Before it, a mistake was permanent, so people worked slowly and carefully. Being able to try something is most of what makes a computer feel safe.

subject: Tech
heading: Your phone has more sensors than a 1990s aircraft
body: Accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, barometer, light, proximity, GPS and several cameras — most of them etched in silicon a few millimetres across.

subject: Making
heading: The paperclip is over a century old and nobody has improved on it
body: The Gem shape was in use by the 1890s. Hundreds of patents have tried to beat it and the plain double loop still holds paper better than any of them.

subject: Making
heading: Concrete from ancient Rome is stronger now than when it was poured
body: Roman harbour concrete used volcanic ash, and seawater reacts with it to grow crystals in the cracks. Modern concrete is destroyed by the same seawater.

subject: Making
heading: Superglue was invented twice by accident and rejected both times
body: It stuck to everything, which was the problem. Its first real use was sealing wounds in Vietnam, before anybody sold it in a tube.

subject: Making
heading: A Swiss Army knife has a tool for a horse’s hoof on some models
body: The hook was for removing stones from hooves. Several tools on older models exist for equipment nobody carries any more and were kept for tradition.

subject: Making
heading: LEGO bricks from 1958 still fit the ones made today
body: The tolerance is about two hundredths of a millimetre. A brick holds roughly 4,000 newtons before it fails — a stack of 375,000 bricks.

subject: Making
heading: The Eiffel Tower is about 15 cm taller in summer
body: Iron expands as it warms. It also leans slightly away from the Sun as one side heats faster than the other.

subject: Making
heading: A violin is held together mostly by glue that is meant to fail
body: Hide glue is used because it can be softened with heat and water, so a two-hundred-year-old instrument can be opened for repair without being destroyed.

subject: Making
heading: Pencils are graded by how much clay is mixed with the graphite
body: More clay makes a harder, lighter line — that is the H. More graphite makes it blacker and softer, which is the B. HB sits in the middle.

subject: Nature
heading: Trees talk to each other through fungi
body: Threads of fungus link roots across a wood and carry sugar, water and chemical warnings. A dying tree can pass its carbon to its neighbours through it.

subject: Nature
heading: Bamboo can grow nearly a metre in a day
body: Some species manage 91 cm in 24 hours. It is a grass, and the whole stem lengthens at once rather than growing from the tip like a tree.

subject: Nature
heading: A single aspen colony in Utah is one of the heaviest living things
body: Pando is about 47,000 stems sharing one root system and one set of genes. Estimates of its age run from thousands to tens of thousands of years.

subject: Nature
heading: Sunflowers follow the Sun only while they are young
body: The stem grows faster on one side to turn the head. Once the flower opens it stops and settles facing east, which warms it early and brings more bees.

subject: Nature
heading: Some plants count
body: A Venus flytrap only shuts after two touches within about twenty seconds, and needs five to start digesting. It is a filter against raindrops.

subject: Nature
heading: Lichen is two organisms living as one
body: A fungus provides the structure and an alga or cyanobacterium provides the food. Some grow less than a millimetre a year and are used to date rock falls.

subject: Nature
heading: Seeds have germinated after two thousand years in a jar
body: A date palm seed from Masada sprouted in 2005. Arctic permafrost has yielded a flowering plant grown from tissue over 30,000 years old.

subject: Nature
heading: Autumn colours were in the leaf all summer
body: The yellows and oranges are carotenoids, hidden by chlorophyll. When the tree stops making chlorophyll before winter, what was underneath shows.

subject: Nature
heading: Moss has no roots
body: It takes water straight through its surface, which is why it grows on stone and why it dries to nothing and revives when it rains.

subject: Weather
heading: No two snowflakes are alike, and one scientist checked for decades
body: Wilson Bentley photographed over 5,000 between 1885 and 1931. Each crystal grows through its own path of temperature and humidity, and the path is the pattern.

subject: Weather
heading: A cloud can weigh as much as a hundred elephants
body: A cumulus a kilometre across holds around 500 tonnes of water, spread as droplets so small that the rising air holds them up.

subject: Weather
heading: Lightning strikes the Earth about 40 times every second
body: Roughly three million strikes a day, most of them over land in the tropics. Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela has storms almost 300 nights a year.

subject: Weather
heading: The largest recorded hailstone was the size of a football
body: One that fell in South Dakota in 2010 measured 20 cm across and weighed nearly a kilogram. Hail grows in layers as it is carried up and down a storm.

subject: Weather
heading: Rain has a smell and it has a name
body: Petrichor: oils from plants collect in dry soil and are thrown into the air by raindrops, along with a compound made by soil bacteria called geosmin.

subject: Weather
heading: A rainbow is a circle and the ground gets in the way
body: From an aeroplane you can see the whole ring. The angle is fixed at about 42 degrees from the point opposite the Sun, which is why nobody reaches the end.

subject: Weather
heading: The wind has a scale invented by a naval officer with no instruments
body: Francis Beaufort described what the sea and the sails looked like at each force. It is still used because a person can read it without a meter.

subject: Weather
heading: Antarctica is a desert
body: The interior gets under 50 mm of precipitation a year, less than the Sahara. Nothing melts, so what falls stays and piles up for millennia.

subject: Weather
heading: Thunder is the sound of air being shoved out of the way
body: The bolt heats a channel of air to about 30,000 degrees in a fraction of a second and it expands supersonically. Count the seconds and divide by three for kilometres.

subject: Money
heading: The pound is the world’s oldest currency still in use
body: It dates from around 775 AD, when a pound of silver was cut into 240 pennies. That is why there were 240 pence in a pound until 1971.

subject: Money
heading: Most money does not exist as notes or coins
body: Around 3% of the money in the UK is physical cash. The rest is numbers in bank ledgers, created when banks make loans.

subject: Money
heading: A £20 note costs a few pence to make
body: Polymer notes cost more than paper ones to print and last two and a half times as long, so they work out cheaper and survive the washing machine.

subject: Money
heading: Compound interest is why starting early beats saving more
body: Save £50 a month from 25 to 35 and stop, or from 35 to 65 at the same rate, and at 7% the first person usually ends up ahead.

subject: Money
heading: The word bankrupt comes from a broken bench
body: Banca rotta in Italian. A money changer who could not pay had his table broken, so nobody would trade at it again.

subject: Money
heading: Cows were money before coins were
body: Cattle, grain and salt were all used. The problem a coin solves is divisibility: you can give half a coin of value, not half a cow.

subject: Money
heading: Britain once taxed windows and people bricked them up
body: The tax ran from 1696 to 1851 and was charged on the number of windows. Blocked-up openings are still visible on Georgian houses.

subject: Sport
heading: A golf ball has dimples because a scuffed ball flew further
body: Players noticed old balls went further than new ones. The dimples trap a thin turbulent layer that keeps the air attached, halving the drag.

subject: Sport
heading: The marathon distance was set by a route to please a royal family
body: The 1908 London Olympics started at Windsor Castle so the children could watch, making 26 miles 385 yards. It was fixed as the standard in 1921.

subject: Sport
heading: A cricket ball swings because one side is polished
body: The smooth side keeps the air attached longer than the rough side, so the pressures differ and the ball curves. Reverse swing happens when the ball is old.

subject: Sport
heading: A table tennis ball spins over a hundred times a second
body: A top player puts enormous topspin on it, which is what makes the ball dive onto the table instead of sailing long. The bat rubber is built for grip.

subject: Sport
heading: The first football World Cup final was played with two different balls
body: Argentina supplied one for the first half and Uruguay one for the second, in 1930. Uruguay won with their own ball on the pitch.

subject: Sport
heading: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver
body: They have been since 1912. The rules require at least six grams of gold plating on a medal that is otherwise about 92% silver.

subject: Sport
heading: A boxing ring is square and the name is older than the rope
body: Fights were held in a circle drawn on the ground with the crowd around it. The square with ropes arrived in 1838 and the word stayed.

subject: Music
heading: Middle C is not in the middle of anything in particular
body: It sits between the treble and bass staves, which is where the name comes from. On a standard 88-key piano it is the fourth C, slightly left of centre.

subject: Music
heading: An octave sounds the same because the frequency doubles
body: The A above middle C is 440 Hz and the next A is 880. Every culture that has been studied treats notes an octave apart as the same note.

subject: Music
heading: The longest piece of music being played will finish in 2640
body: John Cage’s ORGAN2/ASLSP is being performed on a church organ in Halberstadt, Germany. A chord change draws a crowd.

subject: Music
heading: A theremin is played without touching it
body: Two aerials sense the position of the player’s hands by how they change an electrical field. Leon Theremin invented it in 1920 while researching sensors.

subject: Music
heading: A grand piano has around 20 tonnes of string tension
body: That is why the frame is cast iron. The strings pull hard enough that a wooden frame would fold, which is what happened before 1825.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Empire State Building was put up in 410 days
body: It went up during the Depression, about four and a half floors a week, and came in under budget. Steel arrived on site and was bolted in within days.

subject: Buildings
heading: A skyscraper sways on purpose
body: Rigid buildings crack. Tall ones are designed to move up to a metre at the top in high wind, some with a huge weighted pendulum to damp the motion.

subject: Buildings
heading: Notre-Dame took nearly 200 years to build
body: Begun in 1163 and largely finished by 1345. Almost nobody who started it saw it done, which is true of most great cathedrals.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Colosseum could be emptied in about fifteen minutes
body: Eighty numbered entrances and a ticket that told you which stairs to take. Modern stadium design still copies the idea and calls them vomitoria.

subject: Buildings
heading: Some old houses have no thirteenth floor
body: The lifts skip from 12 to 14. Nothing changes about the building; the floor above the twelfth is simply given a different number.

subject: Buildings
heading: Stonehenge’s bluestones came 250 km from Wales
body: Each weighs two to four tonnes. How they were moved around 2500 BC is still argued about, and the quarries have been found in the Preseli Hills.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Sydney Opera House roof was solved by cutting up a sphere
body: Utzon’s design could not be built until he realised every shell could be a piece of one sphere, so the same curve could be cast again and again.

subject: Buildings
heading: Venice is built on millions of wooden piles
body: Driven into the mud, they do not rot because there is no oxygen down there. Over centuries many have partly turned to stone.

subject: People
heading: Marie Curie is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
body: Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes.

subject: People
heading: The man who invented the Pringles tube is buried in one
body: Fredric Baur, a chemist, asked for part of his ashes to be put in a can. His family bought one at a supermarket on the way to the funeral.

subject: People
heading: Alan Turing’s work shortened the Second World War by an estimated two years
body: The Bletchley Park codebreaking effort read German naval signals. The machines built to do it, and the ideas behind them, became the computer.

subject: People
heading: Mary Anning found the first ichthyosaur skeleton at twelve
body: She sold fossils on the Dorset coast to support her family and reshaped palaeontology. The Geological Society did not admit women in her lifetime.

subject: People
heading: Isaac Newton spent more time on alchemy than on physics
body: He also ran the Royal Mint and personally pursued counterfeiters through London. He wrote more words on theology than on mathematics.

subject: People
heading: Nikola Tesla could not stand pearls
body: He refused to speak to a woman wearing them. He also counted his steps, and insisted on hotel room numbers divisible by three.

subject: People
heading: Katherine Johnson checked the computer’s sums by hand
body: John Glenn refused to fly until she had verified the electronic trajectory calculations for his 1962 orbit. She worked at NASA for 33 years.

subject: Oddities
heading: Sweden once drove on the left and swapped overnight
body: At 5 a.m. on 3 September 1967 every vehicle in the country stopped, moved across and started again. Accidents went down for months afterwards.

subject: Oddities
heading: There is a town in Norway with mirrors on the mountains
body: Rjukan sits in a valley with no direct sun for half the year, so in 2013 it installed three steerable mirrors to put a patch of sunlight on the square.

subject: Oddities
heading: A cloud of gas in space smells of raspberries and rum
body: Ethyl formate has been detected near the centre of the galaxy. It is the compound that gives raspberries much of their flavour.

subject: Oddities
heading: The Guinness Book of Records was invented to settle pub arguments
body: A brewery director argued about Europe’s fastest game bird, could not find the answer in any book, and commissioned one in 1954.

subject: Oddities
heading: Bhutan measures Gross National Happiness
body: It has been official policy since the 1970s, with a survey covering health, education, culture and time use. GDP is not the country’s main target.

subject: Oddities
heading: Nobody knows who invented the wheel
body: The oldest evidence is a potter’s wheel from Mesopotamia around 3500 BC. The hard part was never the wheel; it was the axle that had to fit it.

subject: Oddities
heading: A group of crows is called a murder and nobody is sure why
body: The collective nouns come from a 15th-century list written partly as a game for hunters. Many of them were never in ordinary use at all.

subject: Study
heading: Testing yourself beats reading it again, and it is not close
body: Being made to recall something strengthens the memory far more than seeing it. Rereading feels like learning because it feels easy, which is the trap.

subject: Study
heading: Spacing the same hour over a week beats doing it in one go
body: Forgetting a little and pulling it back is what fixes it. Four twenty-minute goes across a week beat one eighty-minute session almost every time.

subject: Study
heading: Mixing topics up feels worse and works better
body: Practising one type of question in a block goes smoothly and fades fast. Shuffling types forces you to work out which method applies, which is the exam skill.

subject: Study
heading: Writing notes by hand beats typing for understanding
body: Typists get more words down and remember less. Writing is slower, so you have to decide what matters, and deciding is the part that sticks.

subject: Study
heading: Sleep is when a memory is filed
body: Learning something and then sleeping beats learning it and staying up, even with the same total study time. A cut-short night undoes part of the day.

subject: Study
heading: Explaining it to somebody is a test in disguise
body: You find the gap the moment you have to say it out loud. An empty chair works: the point is producing the explanation, not who hears it.

subject: Study
heading: Past papers work because they teach the question, not the topic
body: Boards reuse a small set of question shapes. After ten papers you recognise what is being asked before you have finished reading it.

subject: Study
heading: Highlighting is close to useless on its own
body: Study after study finds no benefit. What makes it worth anything is what you do afterwards: turning each highlight into a question you have to answer.

subject: Study
heading: A short break helps more than pushing through
body: Attention fades after about 25 to 40 minutes on hard material. A five-minute break away from a screen resets it; a break on a phone mostly does not.

subject: Study
heading: Working out loud catches mistakes reading silently misses
body: Saying each step names it, and a step you cannot name is usually the one that is wrong. It is why examiners give marks for method.

subject: Study
heading: Cramming works for tomorrow and almost nothing after
body: You can pass a test on material learned last night and have very little of it a fortnight later. For an exam season that is the wrong trade.

subject: Study
heading: Doing the hardest thing first is worth more than it feels
body: Attention and willpower are best early. Leaving the hard question to the end of a session usually means doing it badly or not at all.

subject: Oddities
heading: There is an official unit of measurement called the Smoot
body: A 1958 MIT prank measured a bridge in the height of a student, Oliver Smoot. The markings are repainted every year and the police use them for locations.

subject: Oddities
heading: The shortest commercial flight lasts under two minutes
body: Westray to Papa Westray in Orkney is 2.7 km. With a good wind the aircraft has been recorded doing it in 47 seconds.

subject: Oddities
heading: One Japanese railway station exists for a single passenger
body: Kyu-Shirataki in Hokkaido was kept open for a schoolgirl until she graduated in 2016. The timetable was arranged around her lessons.

subject: Oddities
heading: A cat was once listed as the co-author of a physics paper
body: F.D.C. Willard appeared on a 1975 paper because the author had written "we" throughout and did not want to change it. The cat was his Siamese, Chester.

subject: Oddities
heading: There is a species of jellyfish that can reset to a juvenile
body: Turritopsis dohrnii can turn its cells back into an earlier form when stressed. It can still be eaten, so it is not immortal in any useful sense.

subject: Oddities
heading: The Netherlands has been closing prisons for lack of prisoners
body: Falling crime and a strong preference for community sentences left cells empty. Some have been converted into housing and one into a hotel.

subject: Oddities
heading: Finland gives new parents a cardboard box that is also a cot
body: The maternity package has been issued since 1938 and contains clothes, bedding and a mattress. Infant mortality fell sharply after it was introduced.

subject: Oddities
heading: There is a library of books that cannot be read until 2114
body: The Future Library in Oslo collects one manuscript a year, sealed. A forest was planted in 2014 to supply the paper they will be printed on.

subject: People
heading: Hedy Lamarr co-invented the idea behind Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
body: A film star, she patented frequency hopping in 1942 to stop torpedo signals being jammed. The patent expired before anybody built it.

subject: People
heading: Rosalind Franklin’s photograph is what showed DNA was a helix
body: Photo 51, taken in 1952, was shown to Watson without her knowledge. She died at 37, four years before the Nobel Prize was given for the structure.

subject: People
heading: Ignaz Semmelweis was ignored for telling doctors to wash their hands
body: Deaths on his maternity ward fell from 18% to 2%. He was dismissed, and germ theory arrived twenty years too late to save his reputation.

subject: People
heading: Ada Lovelace saw that a calculating machine could handle more than numbers
body: She wrote that it might compose music if the rules of harmony could be expressed as symbols. Nobody else made that leap for another century.

subject: People
heading: Srinivasa Ramanujan taught himself maths from one textbook
body: He posted his results to Cambridge from a clerk’s job in Madras in 1913. Some of the formulae he sent were not proved for another eighty years.

subject: People
heading: Alexander Fleming found penicillin because he did not tidy up
body: He came back from holiday in 1928 to a contaminated culture plate with a clear ring round the mould. It took another decade to make it into a drug.

subject: Money
heading: A shopkeeper rounding to 99p is using a real effect
body: People read prices left to right and anchor on the first digit. £2.99 is filed as two-something, and the effect survives even when people know about it.

subject: Money
heading: The first cash machine was opened in Enfield in 1967
body: It took a paper voucher impregnated with mildly radioactive carbon-14 and matched it against a PIN. Barclays installed it and Reg Varney used it first.

subject: Money
heading: Inflation is why a 1970s pound would buy about ten pounds of things today
body: Prices in the UK are roughly fourteen times what they were in 1970. It is also why comparing old wages to modern ones without adjusting is meaningless.

subject: Sea
heading: A coral reef is an animal, a plant and a rock at once
body: The polyp is an animal, the algae inside it photosynthesise, and the skeleton it builds is limestone. Bleaching is the polyp expelling its algae under heat stress.

subject: Sea
heading: Jellyfish have no brain, blood or bones
body: A net of nerves runs through the bell and does the work. They have been in the sea for over 500 million years, longer than trees have been on land.

subject: Sea
heading: The sea is not level
body: Gravity varies with the rock below, so the surface sits up to a hundred metres higher in some places than others. Satellites map the bumps to find what is underneath.

subject: Sea
heading: Whales hear each other across ocean basins through a sound channel
body: At a certain depth sound bends back on itself instead of escaping, so a low call travels for hundreds of kilometres. Submarines use the same layer.

subject: Sea
heading: A tsunami is barely a ripple in deep water
body: It may be under a metre high and hundreds of kilometres long, moving at the speed of a jet. It only rears up when the sea floor rises beneath it.

subject: Sea
heading: Seahorse fathers carry the pregnancy
body: The female deposits eggs into a pouch on his belly and he carries them to term. They also pair for life in several species and greet each other daily.

subject: Food
heading: Cheese is a way of keeping milk for the winter
body: Everything about it — salt, acid, drying, mould — is preservation. What we taste as flavour is mostly the controlled result of stopping milk from spoiling.

subject: Food
heading: Every vanilla flower in the world is pollinated by hand
body: The orchid is Mexican and its natural pollinator does not live where vanilla is grown. Each flower opens for one day and must be pollinated that morning.

subject: Food
heading: Most of a cucumber is water and so is most of you
body: A cucumber is about 96% water and an adult human about 60%. Lettuce, celery and watermelon are all above 90%.

subject: Food
heading: Bitterness is a warning system
body: Humans have around 25 different bitter receptors and only one for sweet. Most natural poisons taste bitter, so the tongue is built to be suspicious.

subject: Food
heading: Cooking is what let human brains get big
body: Heat breaks down starch and protein, so a cooked meal gives far more usable energy for the same chewing. Our jaws and guts shrank as our brains grew.

subject: Food
heading: Bread, beer and paper all start with the same trick
body: Breaking long molecules into short ones — starch into sugar, wood into fibre. Enzymes, yeast and heat are the three tools and every kitchen uses all three.

subject: Music
heading: Perfect pitch is more common where the language is tonal
body: In Mandarin and Vietnamese the pitch of a syllable changes the word, so children learn to attend to absolute pitch before the window closes.

subject: Music
heading: A minor chord sounds sad in some cultures and not in others
body: The physics is the same everywhere; the meaning is learned. Listeners with no exposure to Western music do not reliably hear minor as sad.

subject: Music
heading: The loudest instrument in an orchestra is the one at the back
body: A trumpet or trombone can reach over 110 decibels at the player’s ear. Orchestral players are among the professions most at risk of hearing damage.

subject: Music
heading: Singing in a group synchronises heartbeats
body: Choir members’ heart rates line up within minutes, because the breathing pattern of the phrases controls the pulse through the vagus nerve.

subject: Music
heading: The pitch orchestras tune to has been creeping up for centuries
body: Baroque orchestras often used A at 415 Hz; the standard is 440 and some orchestras play at 443. Brighter sounds better, and everyone else has to follow.

subject: Weather
heading: Tornado Alley is moving east
body: The centre of US tornado activity has shifted from the plains towards the Mississippi valley over recent decades, where there are more trees and more people.

subject: Weather
heading: Fog is a cloud that is touching the ground
body: There is no difference in the physics. It forms when air cools to its dew point, which is why valleys and riversides fill first on a clear night.

subject: Weather
heading: Frost can form when the air is above freezing
body: The ground radiates heat to a clear sky and drops below zero while the air a metre up does not. That is why a car roof frosts and the pavement does not.

subject: Weather
heading: Hurricanes spin opposite ways in the two hemispheres
body: The Coriolis effect turns moving air right in the north and left in the south. It is also why one never forms on the equator, where the effect is zero.

subject: Sport
heading: A football swerves because it drags air round with it
body: Spin makes the air faster on one side than the other, so the pressure differs and the ball curves. The same effect makes a cricket ball and a tennis ball dip.

subject: Sport
heading: The high jump was changed by one man going over backwards
body: Dick Fosbury won gold in 1968 with a technique everybody thought was a joke. It lets the body’s centre of mass pass under the bar.

subject: Sport
heading: Swimmers shave because it genuinely helps
body: Removing body hair reduces drag and, by several studies, changes the feel of the water enough to alter stroke length. The gain is small and races are small.

subject: Sport
heading: Marathon runners hit a wall at about 20 miles for a chemical reason
body: The body stores roughly 2,000 calories of glycogen and a marathon costs about 2,600. When it runs out the body switches to fat, which burns far more slowly.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Shard has more glass than a football pitch
body: 11,000 panes covering about 56,000 square metres. The panes are angled so the building reflects the sky and changes colour with the weather.

subject: Buildings
heading: A cathedral spire is a lightning rod that predates the idea
body: Being the tallest thing for miles, they were struck constantly and often burned. Franklin’s rod in 1752 was resisted partly on theological grounds.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Pantheon’s dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome
body: Nearly 1,900 years old, 43 m across, and the concrete gets lighter towards the top — heavy basalt at the base, light pumice at the crown.

subject: Buildings
heading: Medieval builders worked to a drawing scratched on a floor
body: Tracing floors survive at York and Wells: full-size plaster surfaces where the mason cut out the shape of a window before carving the stone.

subject: Making
heading: A saw cuts on the push in Europe and the pull in Japan
body: A pull stroke keeps the blade in tension, so it can be much thinner and takes less wood. A push saw must be stiff enough not to buckle.

subject: Making
heading: Damascus steel was lost for two centuries and is still argued about
body: The patterned blades stopped being made around 1750. Modern analysis found carbon nanotubes in them, probably from impurities in a particular ore.

subject: Making
heading: Bricks are laid in patterns for strength, not decoration
body: A stretcher bond staggers the joints so a crack cannot run straight down. English bond alternates whole bricks across the wall to tie the two skins together.

subject: Making
heading: A nail holds by friction and a screw holds by thread
body: Which is why a nail is better in shear and a screw is better in tension, and why a floorboard is screwed and a rafter is nailed.

subject: Nature
heading: A beaver dam can be seen from space
body: One in Alberta is about 850 m long and was spotted on satellite imagery in 2007. Beavers build in response to the sound of running water.

subject: Nature
heading: Fungi are closer to animals than to plants
body: They cannot photosynthesise, they store food as glycogen the way we do, and their cell walls are made of chitin, the same material as an insect shell.

subject: Nature
heading: The largest organism on Earth may be a fungus in Oregon
body: One honey fungus spreads across nearly 10 square kilometres of forest floor and is thought to be at least 2,400 years old.

subject: Nature
heading: Grass survives being eaten because it grows from the bottom
body: The growing point sits at ground level rather than the tip, so mowing or grazing removes old leaf and not the factory. That is why lawns work.

subject: Earth
heading: Magnetic north wanders and has sped up
