body: It has moved from Canada towards Siberia at up to 55 km a year. Aviation charts and phone compasses are corrected for it on a schedule.

subject: Earth
heading: The Earth’s magnetic field has flipped hundreds of times
body: The last reversal was about 780,000 years ago. Rock forming at the mid-ocean ridge records each flip as a stripe, which is how plate tectonics was proved.

subject: Earth
heading: A river can change country
body: The Rio Grande has moved enough to shift the US-Mexico border, and Italy and Switzerland agreed to redraw theirs as a glacier retreated.

subject: Earth
heading: Soil takes centuries to make and minutes to lose
body: A centimetre of topsoil can take several hundred years to form from rock and organic matter, and a single storm on bare ground can wash it away.

subject: Everyday
heading: Mirrors are slightly green
body: Ordinary glass absorbs a little red and blue. Put two mirrors facing each other and the reflections get greener the further down the tunnel you look.

subject: Everyday
heading: A bar of soap works by having two ends
body: One end of the molecule sticks to water and the other to grease. Rinsing pulls the whole lot away, which is also how washing up liquid and shampoo work.

subject: Everyday
heading: Keys are cut to a code, not to a shape
body: Each cut is one of a small number of depths, so a key is really a short number. That is why a locksmith can cut one from the code stamped on the lock.

subject: Everyday
heading: Road signs are reflective because of millions of tiny glass beads
body: They send light straight back to where it came from, which is why a sign is bright to a driver and dull to somebody standing beside the road.

subject: Everyday
heading: Zips were sold for twenty years before clothes used them
body: They went on boots and tobacco pouches first. The name came from the sound, and clothing makers only adopted them for children’s wear in the 1930s.

subject: Language
heading: Most of the world’s languages have never been written down
body: Of roughly 7,000 living languages, over half have no written tradition. About one dies every few weeks as the last fluent speaker does.

subject: Language
heading: The word deadline probably comes from a prison camp
body: A line around a Civil War camp beyond which prisoners were shot. The printing sense arrived later, and the ordinary one later still.

subject: Language
heading: Reading silently was once considered strange
body: Augustine wrote about Ambrose reading without moving his lips as a curiosity. Word spacing arrived in the 7th century and made silent reading normal.

subject: Space
heading: Uranus rolls round the Sun on its side
body: Its axis is tipped 98 degrees, probably by an ancient collision. Each pole gets 42 years of continuous sunlight and then 42 years of night.

subject: Space
heading: A black hole is not a hole and does not suck
body: It is mass in a very small space. Replace the Sun with a black hole of the same mass and the Earth would carry on in exactly the same orbit, in the dark.

subject: Space
heading: Saturn’s rings are mostly ice and mostly thinner than a house
body: They run 280,000 km across and are typically about ten metres deep. Scaled to a sheet of paper, the rings would be a kilometre wide.

subject: Maths
heading: Every number can be reached by a game nobody can prove ends
body: The Collatz rule: halve it if even, treble and add one if odd. Every number tried lands on 1, and after ninety years nobody has proved they all do.

subject: Maths
heading: A perfect shuffle eight times puts a deck back exactly as it started
body: Split the deck precisely in half and interleave it. Magicians use it; the maths is a permutation of order eight on 52 cards.

subject: Maths
heading: The chance of two people in a room of 60 sharing a birthday is 99%
body: It is the same arithmetic as the 23 case and it still surprises people. Anything below certainty needs 366 people, which is the fact intuition reaches for.

subject: Maths
heading: Prime numbers keep your bank details safe
body: Multiplying two large primes is instant; finding them again from the answer is not. Public key encryption is built on that gap being real.

subject: Body
heading: Your ears and nose never really stop growing
body: Cartilage keeps adding cells slowly, and gravity stretches it. It is why noses and ears are a reasonable guess at somebody’s age.

subject: Body
heading: You blink about 15 times a minute and see no gap
body: The brain suppresses vision during the blink and stitches the two sides together. You lose around 10% of your waking hours to blinks you never noticed.

subject: Body
heading: A shiver is your muscles burning fuel for heat
body: They contract against each other so the energy comes out as warmth rather than movement. It can raise heat production by five times for a short while.

subject: Science
heading: Ice has more than a dozen different crystal forms
body: The one on a pond is ice I. Under pressure water freezes into denser arrangements, and some of them stay solid at temperatures well above boiling.

subject: Science
heading: Static shock is electrons that jumped
body: Rubbing moves electrons from one material to the other. The spark is a few thousand volts and almost no current, which is why it stings and does not harm.

subject: Science
heading: A candle flame is mostly soot glowing
body: The yellow light is solid carbon particles heated until they shine. In zero gravity there is no rising hot air, so a flame is a small blue sphere.

subject: Science
heading: You can boil water at room temperature
body: Boiling is when vapour pressure matches the surrounding pressure. Pump the air out of a jar and water bubbles cold, which is why kettles take longer up a mountain.

subject: Animals
heading: Giraffes have the same number of neck bones as you
body: Seven, like almost every mammal. Each one is just very long, which is also why a giraffe needs a valve system to stop blackouts when it lifts its head.

subject: Animals
heading: Cows have best friends and get stressed when separated
body: Heart rate and cortisol both rise when a cow is penned away from her preferred partner. Dairy herds handled in stable groups produce more milk.

subject: Animals
heading: A starfish has no brain and can eat outside its body
body: It pushes its stomach out through its mouth, digests a mussel inside the shell and pulls the stomach back in. Its nervous system is a ring with no centre.

subject: History
heading: The pyramids were built by paid workers, not slaves
body: Their village has been excavated: bakeries, breweries, medical care for broken bones, and graves near the pyramids, which no slave would have been given.

subject: History
heading: The Great Wall is not one wall and is not visible from space
body: It is many walls built over 2,000 years by different dynasties. At a few metres wide and the colour of the ground, no astronaut has picked it out unaided.

subject: History
heading: Britain switched calendars and lost eleven days
body: In September 1752 the 2nd was followed by the 14th. The tax year still starts on 6 April because the old year end was shifted rather than shortened.

subject: Tech
heading: Every photograph on your phone is a guess
body: The sensor records only one colour per pixel behind a chequered filter, and software works out the other two by comparing neighbours.

subject: Tech
heading: Aeroplane mode exists mostly because of the ground
body: A phone at altitude reaches many masts at once and confuses the network more than it bothers the aircraft. Modern cabins now carry their own small mast.

subject: Tech
heading: The internet is mostly cables under the sea
body: Over 95% of international traffic goes through fibre on the sea bed, not satellites. The bundles are about as thick as a garden hose.

subject: Nature
heading: A dandelion seed flies on a ring of air
body: The bristles create a stable vortex above the seed rather than acting like a parachute. It was only properly explained in 2018.

subject: Nature
heading: Plants defend themselves with chemicals and warn the neighbours
body: Damaged leaves release volatile compounds, and nearby plants of the same species start making their own defences before anything has touched them.

subject: Earth
heading: Gold on Earth mostly arrived after the planet formed
body: Iron dragged the original gold into the core. What can be mined is thought to have been delivered by asteroid bombardment afterwards.

subject: Weather
heading: The jet stream is why flying west takes longer
body: A ribbon of wind at 200 km/h or more runs west to east at cruising height. London to New York is routinely an hour longer than the return.

subject: Money
heading: A credit card number checks itself
body: The last digit is worked out from the others by a rule called the Luhn algorithm, so a typo is caught before anything is sent anywhere.

subject: Buildings
heading: The tallest building has a spire you cannot go up
body: The top 244 m of the Burj Khalifa is unoccupiable structure. Height is measured to the architectural top, so spires are how records are broken.

subject: Everyday
heading: A tea bag was invented by accident as a sample pouch
body: A New York merchant sent loose tea in silk bags in 1908 and customers dropped the whole bag in. He had meant them to open it.

subject: Sport
heading: Chess has more possible games than atoms in the universe
body: The Shannon number puts sensible games at around 10 to the power 120. After four moves each there are already over 288 billion positions.

subject: Oddities
heading: Switzerland has bunkers for its entire population
body: Shelter space is required by law for every resident and has been since 1963. Many are now used as wine cellars, museums, youth hostels and data centres.
